paras: The lynching of Bob Bonner took place at Petersburg, Tennessee, on the night of Friday, November 16, 1888, when five armed masked men took Bonner, a Black prisoner, from the town jail and hanged him half a mile from town. He had been arrested the night before on a charge of outraging a twelve-year-old Black girl. A Nashville wire brief carried the news to papers from Virginia to Minnesota and New Hampshire, while a Tennessee weekly called it "a first class lynching."

According to the Nashville dispatch, Bonner, described as "colored," was arrested on Thursday night, November 15, charged with outraging a twelve-year-old "colored girl." Nothing in the coverage names the girl or describes the evidence behind the charge.

On Friday night five armed and masked men took Bonner from the jail at Petersburg. They hanged him about half a mile from town. The McMinnville Southern Standard added that he was "left hanging nearly all Saturday."
No report of an inquest, arrests or a grand jury inquiry appears in the coverage. The Southern Standard wrote that "the colored people have little sympathy for such members of their race."

Most of the coverage came from a single Nashville dispatch dated November 17, which the Richmond Daily Times printed among its "Brief Telegrams" on November 18. On November 19 the St. Paul Daily Globe ran it under the headline "Lynched by a Masked Quintette," spelling the name "Bonnor," and the Rock Island Daily Argus ran it as "A Tennessee Lynching." The Washington Evening Star printed it the same day in a column of news briefs, and the Concord People and Patriot included it on November 22 in a column of crime items headed "Criminal." These versions kept the wire's wording that Bonner had been arrested "on a charge" of outrage and made no comment on the hanging.

The only Tennessee report found took a different line. In its issue of December 1, the Southern Standard of McMinnville announced that "Petersburg had a first class lynching last Friday," stated as fact that "a negro outraged a 12-year-old girl," and did not name him. Its closing remark presented the lynching as accepted by Black residents.

bases: Five armed masked men took a jailed man accused of rape from the Petersburg jail and hanged him outside town (A1, A3, A6).

Bonner was hanged by five armed masked men who took him from jail with no lawful authority (A1, A3), in response to a charge of outraging a twelve-year-old girl, which the Tennessee paper called 'a first class lynching' (A6).

The Nashville wire (A1, A3, reprinted in A2, A4, A5) and the separate Southern Standard note, which adds details the wire lacks (A6), agree on a Friday-night hanging at Petersburg of a Black man accused of outraging a twelve-year-old girl.

accounts.label: Nashville wire report
accounts.gist: Five armed masked men took Bob Bonner (colored) from jail at Petersburg on Friday night and hanged him half a mile from town; he had been arrested Thursday night on a charge of outraging a twelve-year-old colored girl.

accounts.label: Southern Standard (McMinnville, Tenn.)
accounts.gist: Petersburg 'had a first class lynching last Friday'; a 'negro outraged a 12-year-old girl', was hung Friday night and left hanging nearly all Saturday, and the colored people had little sympathy for him.

framing.detail: Northern and Washington papers ran the Nashville wire as a one-paragraph brief, with headlines such as 'Lynched by a Masked Quintette' and 'A Tennessee Lynching', calling the accusation a 'charge'.
The Southern Standard called it 'a first class lynching', stated the outrage as fact, and said the colored people had little sympathy for 'such members of their race'.

conflicts.note: Most copies of the same wire spell it Bonner; Bonnor in one is likely a typesetting variant.
